analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.15 an hour and extends it to the Northern Mariana Islands.
analysis.headline: The minimum wage bill, backed by 151 House cosponsors, never left committee and got no vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage in two steps, to $5.65 an hour in September 1999 and $6.15 an hour in September 2000, up from $5.15 [S2][S3]. It also would have applied federal minimum wage rules to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, a U.S. territory that had been exempt [S2][S3]. The bill was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to a subcommittee, where no further action was taken [S5]. It died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001 without a floor vote [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the minimum wage would see their hourly pay rise $1.00 by 2000 [S2][S3]. The Congressional Minimum Wage Amendment of the time would also cover workers in the Northern Mariana Islands, where federal wage rules had not previously applied [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.65 an hour in the year starting September 1, 1999, and to $6.15 an hour starting September 1, 2000 [S2][S3].
It extends the federal minimum wage to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, whose workers were previously outside the federal wage floor [S2][S3].
The bill had 151 cosponsors at introduction, showing substantial declared support in the House [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay the minimum wage — concentrated in restaurants, retail, and other low-wage service and manufacturing work — would bear higher payroll costs. In the Northern Mariana Islands, the garment industry's business model relied on wage rates below the federal minimum.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers, including CNMI garment factories

drawbacks.text: Higher mandated wages raise labor costs for small businesses and low-margin employers, who may respond with price increases, reduced hours, or slower hiring; this is the standard economic trade-off of any minimum wage increase.
The increase was a fixed dollar amount ($5.65 then $6.15) rather than indexed to inflation, so the raise would erode over time until Congress acted again [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A $1.00-an-hour raise spread over two years is a modest, predictable increase that millions of low-paid workers would have felt directly. The cost side is higher payroll expenses for employers of minimum-wage labor, which is a real but ordinary trade-off for this policy; the bill contained no offsetting tax relief for small businesses, which was the main Republican objection to similar proposals that Congress.

outcome.mechanism: The House sent the bill to its Education and the Workforce Committee, which routed it to a subcommittee in February 1999; nothing further happened and the bill expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Bonior (D-MI) introduced the Fair Minimum Wage Act on January 19, 1999, with 151 cosponsors (150 Democrats and 1 Independent) [S4][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on January 19, 1999 [S5].
On February 24, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and the record shows no further action [S5].
The bill never received a House floor vote and died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers paying minimum-wage wages kept $5.15 as the federal floor, and the Northern Mariana Islands garment industry kept its exemption from federal wage rules. The federal minimum wage would not rise again until 2007.

for.name: Rep. David Bonior
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited the House Democratic leadership as original cosponsors.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; referred it to a subcommittee where it sat without a hearing or markup.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority control of the House floor agenda
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote; as the bill never left committee, committee inaction was the operative block.

sides.party_line_note: All 151 cosponsors were Democrats or the House's one Independent; the bill died in a committee controlled by Republicans without any recorded vote.

industries.note: A higher federal wage floor raises their payroll costs; their savings from the bill's failure were roughly a dollar an hour per minimum-wage worker. The bill's death meant no offsetting small-business tax relief either.
CNMI factories produced apparel under U.S. trade rules while paying wages below the federal minimum; extending the federal wage floor to the territory would have ended that advantage.
